lessons.title: Lesson 1: What estate planning is, and what a will does
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain what a will does and what can happen without one.
This lesson builds toward: Given the basic estate planning words, you will explain what a will does, what an executor does and what can happen without a will, in your own words, getting at least 4 of 5 questions right.
Estate planning means deciding ahead of time what happens to your money and belongings when you die, and who makes decisions for you if you become too sick to decide. Your estate is everything you own, minus what you owe.
A will is a legal document that says who gets your belongings, and names an executor: the person who carries out your wishes, pays final bills and hands out what is left. In many places a will can also name a guardian for children under 18 in your care, such as grandchildren you are raising.
If you die without a will, the law where you live decides who inherits, and a court picks who handles your estate. The result may not be what you wanted.
Each state and country has its own rules for a will to be valid, such as how it is signed and witnessed. A will that does not follow those rules may not count. That is why this course helps you prepare, and a lawyer or legal aid helps you make it legal.
Words to know:
- Estate: everything you own, such as money, a home, a car and belongings, minus what you owe.
- Will: a legal document that says who gets your belongings after you die and who carries out your wishes.
- Executor: the person named in a will to carry out your wishes and settle your estate.
- Guardian: a person named to care for a child under 18.
Official sources:
- LawHelp.org: find free legal help and information in your state
Try it now: Write down three things that matter most to you to pass on, such as a home, savings, a family Bible, a car or a pet's care, and who you would want to have each one. This is a private list for you, not a legal document.
You can now explain what a will and an executor are, and why a will must follow the rules where you live.

options: The person who carries out the wishes in your will
check.why: The executor carries out your wishes, pays final bills and hands out what is left.

check.q: Your friend says, "I don't need a will; my family will sort it out." What could happen without one?
options: The law where they live decides who inherits, which may not match their wishes
check.why: Without a will, the law decides who inherits and a court picks who handles the estate.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Checking your beneficiaries
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find every account or policy that has a beneficiary and check who is named.
This lesson builds toward: Given your life insurance, retirement and bank accounts, you will check who is named as beneficiary and backup on each one, marking every form that is out of date.
Some money does not go through your will at all. Life insurance, many retirement accounts and pensions, and some bank accounts let you name a beneficiary: the person who gets that money when you die. These forms usually control who gets that money, even if your will says something different.
That is why old forms cause problems. A life insurance policy might still name a former spouse, or a parent who has passed away, or a child before the grandchildren were born.
Make a list of every account and policy you have. For each one, ask the company or check your online account to see who is named as the beneficiary and the backup (often called the contingent beneficiary). Update any that are wrong using the company's own form.
Review your beneficiaries after big life events: a marriage, a divorce, a death, a birth or a new grandchild. Ask a lawyer before naming a minor child or a person who gets disability benefits, because there can be special rules.
Step by step:
- List every life insurance policy, retirement account, pension and bank account.
- For each, find out who is named as beneficiary and as backup.
- Mark any that are out of date.
- Update them with the company's own form.
- Review again after a marriage, divorce, death or birth.
Words to know:
- Beneficiary: the person you name to receive money from an account or policy when you die.
- Contingent beneficiary: the backup who receives the money if the first beneficiary has died.
- Life event: a big change like a marriage, divorce, death or birth.
Official sources:
- CFPB: Managing someone else's money (guides for families)
Try it now: List every account or policy you have that could have a beneficiary. Pick one, check who is named (online, on your paperwork or by calling the company), and write down whether it is still right.
You can now find your accounts that have beneficiaries, check who is named, and know when to update them.

options: The person who writes your will
The person named to get the money from an account or policy when you die
check.why: A beneficiary is the person named on an account or policy to receive that money.

check.q: Your pension form still names your late husband as beneficiary. What do you do?
options: Leave it; the will covers it
Cross out his name on your copy
Update it using the company's own form
check.why: Beneficiary forms usually control who gets that money, so update them with the company's form.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Power of attorney and health care directives
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Explain who would decide for you about money and about health care if you could not.
This lesson builds toward: Given the people in your life, you will choose an executor, a financial agent and a health care agent, with a backup for each, choosing people who are trustworthy, reachable and will follow your wishes.
A will only works after you die. Other documents protect you while you are alive, if an illness or accident leaves you unable to decide for yourself.
A financial power of attorney names an agent: a person you trust to handle money and property for you, such as paying bills or talking to the bank. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has free guides for people who are named as agents. Without one, your family may have to go to court to get a guardian or conservator named, which takes time and money.
A health care directive, also called an advance directive, covers medical decisions. A health care power of attorney (or health care proxy) names a person you trust to make health decisions if you cannot. A living will writes down which treatments you would or would not want if you were dying or permanently unconscious, such as breathing machines or tube feeding.
Choose people who are trustworthy, live close enough or can be reached, and will follow your wishes, not their own. Name a backup for each. Then talk with them, and with your doctor, about what you want. The forms and rules differ by state and country, so get them from a lawyer, legal aid, your doctor's office or hospital, and ask how to sign them correctly.
Words to know:
- Power of attorney: a legal document that lets a person you choose act for you.
- Agent: the person you name in a power of attorney.
- Advance directive: documents that tell doctors and family your health care wishes and who decides for you.
- Living will: a document that says which treatments you want or do not want near the end of life.
- Health care proxy: the person you name to make health decisions if you cannot.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus: Advance directives
- CFPB: Managing someone else's money
Try it now: Write the name of the person you would choose as your financial agent and as your health care proxy, and a backup for each. Next to each name, write one reason you trust them.
You can now explain a financial power of attorney, a health care proxy and a living will, and choose who you trust for each.

check.q: What does a financial power of attorney do?
options: Names someone to handle your money and property if you cannot
Says who gets your house when you die
check.why: A financial power of attorney names an agent to manage money for you while you are alive.

check.q: You are choosing a health care agent. Who is the best choice?
options: Someone you have not seen in years
A trusted person you can reach who will follow your wishes, with a backup
check.why: Choose someone trustworthy, reachable and willing to follow your wishes, and name a backup.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Listing what you own and what you owe
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a simple list of your assets and debts that a lawyer and your family can use.
This lesson builds toward: Using paper or a private file, you will list what you own and what you owe, showing only the last four digits of any number and no passwords.
Before you meet a lawyer, make a list of what you own and what you owe. This list helps the lawyer give good advice, and later helps your executor find everything.
What you own (assets): bank and credit union accounts, retirement accounts and pensions, life insurance, your home or land, vehicles, valuable belongings, and things with family value such as jewelry or photos. Also list online accounts such as email and photo storage, and any pets that need a new home.
What you owe (debts): a mortgage, car loan, credit cards, medical bills and any personal loans.
For each item, write the company and the kind of account, but not full account numbers or passwords. Write "ends in 1234" instead. Keep this list somewhere safe. Do not type it into an AI assistant or email it to anyone who has not been chosen to help you.
Step by step:
- Write a heading: What I own. List accounts, policies, property, vehicles and valued items.
- Add online accounts and pets.
- Write a heading: What I owe. List each debt and who it is with.
- Use only the last four digits of any number, and never write passwords on this list.
- Store it in a safe place.
Words to know:
- Asset: something you own that has value, like money, a home or a car.
- Debt: money you owe, like a mortgage or credit card.
- Inventory: a full list of what you have.
Try it now: Start your list now on paper: write at least five things you own and every debt you have, with the company name and only the last four digits of any number.
You can now make a private, organized list of what you own and owe for your lawyer and family.

options: What you own, such as accounts, property and valued items
check.why: Assets are what you own; debts are what you owe.

check.q: You are writing your savings account on your list. How do you write the number?
check.why: Write only the last four digits, and never write passwords on the list.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Getting ready for a lawyer or legal aid
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find legal help near you and prepare the choices and questions to bring.
This lesson builds toward: Before you meet a lawyer or legal aid, you will find a source of legal help near you and write at least five clear questions, including what it will cost and what is included. Given the people in your life, you will choose an executor, a financial agent and a health care agent, with a backup for each, choosing people who are trustworthy, reachable and will follow your wishes.
Estate planning help does not have to be expensive. Free or low-cost help may come from legal aid groups, senior legal services, law school clinics and volunteer lawyer programs. LawHelp.org lets you choose your state to find free legal help from nonprofit legal aid. The Eldercare Locator (1-800-677-1116) connects older adults and families to local services; ask them about legal help for seniors near you. Your state or local bar association may also have a lawyer referral service.
Online will forms and kits exist, but a form that does not match your state's rules, or your family's situation, can fail. A lawyer or legal aid can tell you whether a simple form is enough for you or not.
Bring what you prepared: your list of what you own and owe, your beneficiary check, and the people you chose for executor, guardian, financial agent and health care proxy, with backups. Also bring questions.
Good questions: Do I need a will, a trust, or both? How should my will be signed and witnessed here? What happens to my home? What should I do about a grandchild in my care? What will this cost, and what is included? An AI assistant can help you write your questions in clear words, but leave out names and numbers, and let the lawyer give the legal answers.
Step by step:
- Go to LawHelp.org and choose your state, or call the Eldercare Locator.
- Ask about free or low-cost estate planning for seniors.
- Gather your lists and the people you chose.
- Write at least five questions.
- Ask what it will cost and what is included before you start.
Words to know:
- Legal aid: free legal help from nonprofit groups for people who qualify.
- Lawyer referral service: a service, often from a bar association, that connects you to a lawyer.
- Trust: a legal arrangement where a person manages property for others; a lawyer can say whether you need one.
Official sources:
- LawHelp.org: Find free legal help
- Eldercare Locator (Administration for Community Living)
Try it now: Go to LawHelp.org, choose your state and find one legal aid group or senior legal service near you. Write its name and phone number, and write five questions you would ask it.
You can now find free or low-cost legal help near you and come to the meeting prepared.

options: A site to find free legal help from nonprofit legal aid in your state
check.why: LawHelp.org lets you choose your state to find free legal help.

check.q: You want AI to help write your questions for the lawyer. What do you leave out?
check.why: AI can help with clear wording, but leave out names and numbers and let the lawyer answer.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Organizing and storing your important papers
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Put your papers in one safe place and tell the right people where they are.
This lesson builds toward: Given your important papers, you will organize them in one folder and write a "where my papers are" note for your family, shared with the people you named.
A plan only helps if people can find it. Many families search for days for a will, an insurance policy or the deed to a house. You can spare them that.
Make one folder or binder. Put in it, or write where to find: your will and other legal documents, your power of attorney and health care directive, your list of what you own and owe, insurance policies, deeds and titles, your Medicare or other health cards (copies), and a contact list: your lawyer, doctor, bank and the people you named.
Ask your lawyer where the signed original of your will should be kept, because the rules and choices differ. Give a copy of your health care directive to your health care proxy and your doctor, so it is there in an emergency. Keep the binder in a safe place at home that your executor knows about.
Write a one-page "where my papers are" note and give it to the people you named. Review everything every few years and after big life events. When you change something, tell your family, and remove old versions so nobody uses the wrong one.
Step by step:
- Make one binder or folder for important papers.
- Add each document, or a note saying where it is.
- Ask your lawyer where to keep the original will.
- Give your health care directive to your proxy and your doctor.
- Write a "where my papers are" note and share it with the people you named.
- Review after big life events and remove old versions.
Words to know:
- Original: the signed document itself, not a copy.
- Deed: the legal paper that shows who owns a home or land.
- Title: the paper that shows who owns a vehicle.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus: Advance directives
Try it now: Final task: build your estate-planning folder with your list of what you own and owe, your beneficiary check, the people you would name with backups, at least five questions for a lawyer or legal aid, and a one-page "where my papers are" note. Then find one legal help office near you and write down how to contact it.
You can now organize your important papers, store them safely and tell the right people where they are.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds What I own and owe The list is missing major items, or shows full account numbers or passwords. A list of assets and debts with the company and kind of account, using only the last four digits. Also lists online accounts and pets, and is stored in a safe place. Beneficiary check Some accounts or policies were not checked. Every account or policy with a beneficiary is listed, with the named person and backup. Out-of-date forms are marked and the update form has been requested. People named One or more roles is missing, or there are no backups. An executor, financial agent and health care agent, each with a backup. Has talked with the people chosen about their role and your wishes. Questions for a lawyer Fewer than five questions, or no source of legal help. At least five clear questions, including cost, and one place near you that offers legal help. Has contacted the legal help or booked an appointment. Where my papers are No note, or it leaves out where key papers are. A one-page note saying where each important paper is. The note has been given to the people named in the plan. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Why give a copy of your health care directive to your doctor?
options: So it is there in an emergency
So the doctor can change it
check.why: Your proxy and doctor need a copy so it is available when it matters.

check.q: You updated your will. What do you do with the old version?
options: Mail the old one to a relative
Follow your lawyer's advice and make sure nobody uses the old one
check.why: Remove old versions so nobody uses the wrong one, and tell your family about the change.
